title: Meet the Other Simpson
text:
How winning in every group can still mean losing overall
Anna Zhao

2026-09-13



Statistics in everyday lifeMeet the Other SimpsonHow winning in every group can still mean losing overall.Anna Zhao   /   600 words of main text   /   4 min read+Have you ever watched The Simpsons? Then here is another Simpson worth meeting: Simpson's paradox. The shared name makes a fun introduction, but this statistical idea has nothing to do with Springfield. It describes a surprising reversal: a pattern appears in every subgroup, yet points the opposite way when those groups are combined. How can both stories be true?1. Two hitters, one surprising scoreboardConsider the baseball example featured on MyPointIs: Derek Jeter and David Justice in 1995 and 1996. A batting average is hits divided by at-bats, the batting opportunities counted in this statistic. Justice leads in both seasons: 25.3% versus 25.0%, then 32.1% versus 31.4%. Who would you expect to lead across both years?

1995-1996 records. Cells show hits / at-bats and percentages.


Period
Derek Jeter
David Justice




1995
12/48 25.0%
104/411 25.3%


1996
183/582 31.4%
45/140 32.1%


Overall
195/630 31%
149/551 27%



Jeter wins the combined comparison: 195 hits from 630 at-bats, or 31.0%, against Justice's 149 from 551, or 27.0%. About 92% of Jeter's opportunities came in 1996, when both players had higher averages. Only about 25% of Justice's came that year. Their combined averages therefore give very different importance to each season.

Justice leads in each season; Jeter leads overall. Every bar starts at zero. MyPointIs example; data.2. When the patient mix changes the winnerThe same reversal appears in published research. A 1986 study by Charig and colleagues compared kidney-stone treatments. Here we focus on open surgery (A) and percutaneous nephrolithotomy (B), which removes stones through a small opening. Success meant eliminating stones or reducing them below two millimetres after three months.

Successes / patients and success rates. Small stones: under 2 cm; large: 2 cm or more. A = open surgery; B = percutaneous nephrolithotomy.


Stone size
Treatment B
Treatment A




Small stones
234/270 86.7%
81/87 93.1%


Large stones
55/80 68.8%
192/263 73.0%


Overall
289/350 82.6%
273/350 78.0%



Overall, B succeeded in 82.6% of cases, compared with 78.0% for A. Yet A had higher success rates within both stone-size groups: 93.1% versus 86.7% for small stones, and 73.0% versus 68.8% for large stones. The winner changes when we combine the groups, just as it did with the baseball players.
Why? Large stones accounted for 263 of A's 350 cases, but only 80 of B's 350. Success was less common for large stones under either treatment. A therefore faced a much heavier concentration of difficult cases. The overall comparison mixes treatment outcomes with differences in the patients being treated.

A leads in both size groups; B leads overall. Charig et al. (1986); subgroup analysis.The hidden ingredient: weightsBoth reversals come from weighted averages. In the formula, g labels a subgroup, r is its success rate, and w is its share of the relevant total. The weights add to one. Each player or treatment has its own weights, reflecting its particular mix of opportunities or cases. An overall result answers what happened in the observed mix; a standardized comparison asks what the rates would look like with the same mix. Both need a clearly stated purpose.Overall rate = ∑g wg × rg∑g wg = 1For treatment A, multiply 81/87 by 87/350, then add 192/263 times 263/350. This gives 273/350, or 78%. Simply averaging the two subgroup percentages would wrongly give small and large stones equal weight. In baseball, the corresponding weights are each season's share of a player's total at-bats.Where this mattersThis matters when interpreting everyday comparisons. In education, school pass rates can reflect differences in students' prior preparation. In business, campaign conversion rates can reflect whether audiences contain mostly returning customers or newcomers. Comparing relevant subgroups and showing their sizes helps readers see what an overall average actually combines.
In research, the practical application is to examine group composition before interpreting a headline result. Researchers can also compare outcomes using a common set of weights, making the target population explicit. But subgroup comparisons alone do not establish causation: the kidney-stone comparison was historical and nonrandomized, so other differences could still matter.Before believing the headlineThe lesson is not to distrust every average or split data endlessly. Choosing useful groups requires understanding the question and when variables were measured. Adjusting for consequences of an intervention can itself introduce bias. Next time a headline offers one impressive number, ask: who is inside it, and who contributes most? Simpson's paradox reminds us that correct numbers can still tell an incomplete story.Source and data note. Conceptual reference: Econometrics I, Week 2, Section 2.14, pp. 20-21. Baseball example: Rachel, MyPointIs (2023), with counts checked against Illustrative Mathematics. Kidney-stone research: Charig et al., BMJ (1986), doi:10.1136/bmj.292.6524.879; subgroup analysis: Julious & Mullee, BMJ (1994), doi:10.1136/bmj.309.6967.1480. Percentages are recalculated from counts (234/270 = 86.7%). This is a historical illustration, not current treatment advice. Education and business applications describe possibilities, not specific studies. Main-text word count excludes headings, tables, captions, formula, and this note.

title: Meet the other Simpson–The Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Kidney-stone research example
A study of kidney-stone treatments shows the same problem. In 1986, Charig and his colleagues compared several treatments. Here, Treatment A means open surgery. Here we focus on open surgery (A) and percutaneous nephrolithotomy (B), which removes stones through a small opening. Success meant eliminating stones or reducing them below two millimetres after three months.

Successes / patients and success rates. Small stones: under 2 cm; large: 2 cm or more. A = open surgery; B = percutaneous nephrolithotomy.




Stone size
Treatment B
Treatment A




Small stones
234/270 (86.7%)
81/87 (93.1%)


Large stones
55/80 (68.8%)
192/263 (73.0%)


Overall
289/350 (82.6%)
273/350 (78.0%)



Overall, Treatment B succeeded in 82.6% of cases, compared with 78.0% for Treatment A. Yet A had higher success rates within both stone-size groups: 93.1% versus 86.7% for small stones, and 73.0% versus 68.8% for large stones. The winner changes when we combine the groups, same as the baseball players example.
Why? Large stones accounted for 263 of A’s 350 cases, but only 80 of B’s 350. Success was less common for large stones under either treatment. Treatment A, therefore, faced a much heavier concentration of difficult cases. The overall comparison mixes treatment outcomes with differences in the patients being treated.

title: Meet the other Simpson–The Simpson’s Paradox
text:
The hidden aspect: weights
Both reversals come from weighted averages. In the formula, g labels a subgroup, r is its success rate, and w is its share of the relevant total. The weights add to one. Each player or treatment has its own weights, reflecting its particular mix of opportunities or cases. An overall result answers what happened in the observed mix; a standardized comparison asks what the rates would look like with the same mix. Both need a clearly stated purpose.
\[\text{Overall rate}
= \sum_{g=1}^{G} w_g r_g,
\qquad
\sum_{g=1}^{G} w_g = 1\]

title: Meet the other Simpson–The Simpson’s Paradox
text:
Why this Matter?
Simpson’s paradox matters. A school’s pass rate may partly reflect how prepared its students were before they arrived. An advertising campaign may reach more returning customers than another campaign. Looking only at the overall results can hide these differences. Looking at group sizes helps us understand what we are comparing.
In research, the application is to examine group composition before interpreting a headline result. Researchers can also compare outcomes using a common set of weights, making the target population explicit. But subgroup comparisons alone do not establish causation: the kidney-stone comparison was historical and nonrandomized, so other differences could still matter.
For me, the key point is to rethink before trusting a single average. Who is included? Which group makes up most of the total? Does the pattern change when we look deeper? Simpson’s paradox reminds us that correct numbers can still tell an incomplete story.
